clues.text: Mason Gerd writes: 'I keep my eyes on the hills, but I want to learn what lies beyond them. Go to Hesper, who keeps the maps, and fetch one for me.'
clues.redirect: No shelves of old records are kept here. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.object:notice-board: Signs are pinned up on this for passers-by, but nothing is shelved here. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: Gerd wants a map, and Hesper keeps the maps in the library.

clues.text: Carpenter Aldo writes: 'The planks are fixed, but I cannot see if more storms are coming. Ask the one who keeps the lantern up high to look out for me.'
clues.redirect: No lantern keeps watch on the hills from here. What does the writer want?

redirects.landmark:puzzle-tower: This tall place is full of puzzles, not a lookout. What does the writer want?

clues.why: Aldo asks for the lookout with the lantern up high: the watchtower.

clues.text: Sister Wren writes: 'I need sprigs of lavender to sweeten the air for my visitors. Keeper Ivy will spare some from her sunny beds.'
clues.redirect: No herbs grow here. Read the note again.

redirects.object:beehives: These hives are homes for buzzing workers, not herb beds. Read the note again.

clues.why: Wren sends you to Keeper Ivy's sunny beds: the garden.

clues.text: Crier Pip writes: 'Tomorrow I must announce the lord's return. Wait at the end of the north road, where he will ride in through the great doors.'
clues.redirect: This is not where the north road ends. Which place fits every part of the note?
clues.why: The great doors at the end of the north road are the castle gate.

clues.text: Hesper writes: 'My books hold many riddles, but the trickiest bonus ones wait in stone at the south-east edge. Go and try them.'
clues.redirect: There are no bonus puzzles here. What does the writer want?

redirects.landmark:watchtower: This is Mason Gerd's lookout over the hills, not a place of puzzles. What does the writer want?

clues.why: Bonus riddles in stone at the south-east edge are the Puzzle Tower's.

clues.text: Crier Pip writes: 'I cannot shout loud enough for everyone, so I have pinned my message where travellers enter from the south.'
clues.redirect: Nothing is pinned up here for passers-by. Read the note again.

redirects.landmark:library: Hesper keeps her shelves here, but nobody pins up signs. Read the note again.

clues.why: Pip's message is pinned where travellers enter from the south: the notice board.

clues.text: Old Bram writes: 'My pails are for people. Lead those thirsty horses to the long wooden basin at the south edge instead.'
clues.redirect: This is not where the animals stop for a slurp. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.landmark:well: Old Bram fills pails for people here, not for animals. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: Bram sends the horses to the long wooden basin for animals: the water trough.

clues.text: Keeper Ivy writes: 'My herbs need visitors from the wooden homes at the south-west edge. Go and thank those buzzing workers for me.'
clues.redirect: No stinging workers live here. What does the writer want?

redirects.landmark:garden: This is Keeper Ivy's place of herbs, not the workers' homes. What does the writer want?

clues.why: Ivy's buzzing visitors live in wooden homes at the south-west edge: the beehives.

clues.text: The stable boy writes: 'The ponies refused their oats today. They only want the dry grass heaped on wheels at the east edge.'
clues.redirect: There is no hay here. Read the note again.
clues.why: Dry grass heaped on wheels at the east edge is the hay cart.

clues.text: A traveller writes: 'In the city we buy water by the cup. Here, I am told, an old man draws it up free for every doorstep.'
clues.redirect: Old Bram does not fill pails here. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.object:water-trough: This trough is for the animals, not for people's kettles. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: Water drawn up for every doorstep by Old Bram comes from the well; the trough is for animals.

clues.text: Crier Pip writes: 'Today I announce that the baker will have flour again, thanks to Tessa's mended stones. Go and thank her.'
clues.redirect: No grain is ground into flour here. What does the writer want?
clues.why: Tessa's stones make the baker's flour at the mill.

clues.text: Old Bram writes: 'I have never trusted that rushing current. Thank goodness for the timbers Aldo keeps sound. Meet me halfway across.'
clues.redirect: This does not take you over the river. Read the note again.
clues.why: Timbers over the current, kept by Carpenter Aldo, are the bridge.

clues.text: Mason Gerd writes: 'From my post I hear it every evening, a voice of bronze calling people to be still. Go where it hangs.'
clues.redirect: No bell calls anyone to be still here. Which place fits every part of the note?
clues.why: A voice of bronze that calls people to be still is a bell, and it hangs in the chapel.

clues.text: Miller Tessa writes: 'My flour becomes loaves, and the loaves are sold where Crier Pip sings out. Go and buy one.'
clues.redirect: No one buys or sells at stalls here. What does the writer want?
clues.why: Loaves are sold where Crier Pip calls: the market.

clues.text: Sister Wren writes: 'I need the words of an old hymn. Hesper will know which shelf holds them.'
clues.redirect: No shelves of old records are kept here. Read the note again.

redirects.object:notice-board: Signs are pinned up on this for passers-by, but nothing is shelved here. Read the note again.

clues.why: Hesper's shelves are in the library.

clues.text: Keeper Ivy writes: 'Frost may come tonight and kill my herbs. Ask the one who watches the hills from up high to send word if the sky clears.'
clues.redirect: No lantern keeps watch on the hills from here. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.landmark:puzzle-tower: This tall place is full of puzzles, not a lookout. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: The one who watches the hills from up high is at the watchtower.

clues.text: Miller Tessa writes: 'After a dusty day at the stones, I rest on the sunny bench among the herbs. Bring my lunch there.'
clues.redirect: No herbs grow here. What does the writer want?

redirects.object:beehives: These hives are homes for buzzing workers, not herb beds. What does the writer want?

clues.why: A sunny bench among herbs is in the garden.

clues.text: Mason Gerd writes: 'From up high I can see riders coming to the keep. Meet them where the north road ends and let them in.'
clues.redirect: This is not where the north road ends. Read the note again.
clues.why: Riders enter the castle where the north road ends: the castle gate.

clues.text: An unsigned riddle: 'I am the voice that tells the village when to be still. I hang above a house of hush, and Sister Wren keeps me polished. Go where I hang.'
clues.redirect: No bell calls anyone to be still here. What does the writer want?
clues.why: A voice that calls for stillness is a bell, and it hangs in Sister Wren's quiet chapel.

clues.text: An unsigned riddle: 'Feed me gold and I give back white. My stone teeth never tire, and the baker would starve without me.'
clues.redirect: No grain is ground into flour here. Read the note again.
clues.why: Gold grain goes in and white flour comes out between grinding stones: the mill.

clues.text: An unsigned riddle: 'I am deep and dark, and an old man winds my rope. Every doorstep owes me its full kettle.'
clues.redirect: Old Bram does not fill pails here. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.object:water-trough: This trough is for the animals, not for people's kettles. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: A deep, dark shaft whose rope Old Bram winds, filling every kettle, is the well.

clues.text: An unsigned riddle: 'I hold travellers above the current, rain or shine. A carpenter keeps my planks sound. Go and stand on me.'
clues.redirect: This does not take you over the river. What does the writer want?
clues.why: Planks above the current that hold in any weather are the bridge.

clues.text: Carry this grumble to the place it is about: 'Fiddles at dawn, haggling till dusk, and the crier shouting prices! How can anyone think in that square?'
clues.redirect: No one buys or sells at stalls here. Read the note again.
clues.why: Fiddles, haggling and a crier calling prices fill the market square.

clues.text: An unsigned riddle: 'Hush. I hold more tales than any person could tell in a lifetime, each in its own place on a shelf. Hesper guards me.'
clues.redirect: No shelves of old records are kept here. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.object:notice-board: Signs are pinned up on this for passers-by, but nothing is shelved here. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: Tales kept on shelves and guarded by Hesper are in the library.

clues.text: Carry this grumble to the place it is about: 'That lantern up high burns all night, and the mason will not put it out. He says the hills must be watched.'
clues.redirect: No lantern keeps watch on the hills from here. What does the writer want?

redirects.landmark:puzzle-tower: This tall place is full of puzzles, not a lookout. What does the writer want?

clues.why: A lantern burning all night so the hills are watched is the watchtower's.

clues.text: An unsigned riddle: 'I smell of thyme and sage, my bench soaks up the sun, and Keeper Ivy pulls my weeds.'
clues.redirect: No herbs grow here. Read the note again.

redirects.object:beehives: These hives are homes for buzzing workers, not herb beds. Read the note again.

clues.why: Herbs, a sunny bench and Keeper Ivy mean the garden.

clues.text: Carry this grumble to the place it is about: 'I walked the north road to its very end, only to find the great doors to the keep shut until dawn.'
clues.redirect: This is not where the north road ends. Which place fits every part of the note?
clues.why: The great doors to the castle at the end of the north road are the castle gate.

clues.text: Carry this boast to the place it is about: 'I climbed the stone steps at the south-east edge and solved every bonus puzzle inside. Bet you can't!'
clues.redirect: There are no bonus puzzles here. What does the writer want?

redirects.landmark:watchtower: This is Mason Gerd's lookout over the hills, not a place of puzzles. What does the writer want?

clues.why: Bonus puzzles up stone steps at the south-east edge are in the Puzzle Tower.

clues.text: Carry this grumble from Crier Pip to the place it is about: 'Everyone reads the signs by the southern entrance now, and nobody listens to me!'
clues.redirect: Nothing is pinned up here for passers-by. Read the note again.

redirects.landmark:library: Hesper keeps her shelves here, but nobody pins up signs. Read the note again.

clues.why: The signs by the southern entrance are pinned on the notice board; nothing is pinned at the library.

clues.text: Carry this grumble from Old Bram to the place it is about: 'Those oxen splashed my clean pails again! They have their own long wooden basin at the south edge.'
clues.redirect: This is not where the animals stop for a slurp. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.landmark:well: Old Bram fills pails for people here, not for animals. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: The oxen's own long wooden basin at the south edge is the water trough.

clues.text: A warning found on the south-west path: 'Walk softly. The little striped workers in the wooden boxes here do not like visitors.' Go where it points.
clues.redirect: No stinging workers live here. What does the writer want?

redirects.landmark:garden: This is Keeper Ivy's place of herbs, not the workers' homes. What does the writer want?

clues.why: Little striped workers in wooden boxes on the south-west edge live in the beehives.

clues.text: Carry this boast to the place it is about: 'I forked every bit of that dry grass onto the wagon at the east edge, all by myself!'
clues.redirect: There is no hay here. Read the note again.
clues.why: Dry grass forked onto a wagon at the east edge is the hay cart.

clues.text: Carry this thank-you to the place it is meant for: 'Old friend, your rope and pail have filled my kettle every morning for forty years.'
clues.redirect: Old Bram does not fill pails here. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.object:water-trough: This trough is for the animals, not for people's kettles. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: A rope and pail that fill a kettle every morning belong to the well.

clues.text: Carry this grumble from the baker to the place it is about: 'Late again! I cannot bake a crumb until Tessa's stones have done their work.'
clues.redirect: No grain is ground into flour here. What does the writer want?
clues.why: Tessa's stones grind the baker's flour at the mill.

clues.text: Carry this grumble from the ferryman to the place it is about: 'Since that carpenter's crossing went up, nobody needs my boat.'
clues.redirect: This does not take you over the river. Read the note again.
clues.why: The carpenter's crossing over the river is the bridge.

clues.text: Carry this thank-you to the place it is meant for: 'After the noise of the road, your hush and your bell were a gift, Sister.'
clues.redirect: No bell calls anyone to be still here. Which place fits every part of the note?
clues.why: Sister Wren's quiet place with a bell is the chapel.

clues.text: Carry this thank-you to the place it is meant for: 'Pip, your crowd was the best I have ever played for, and the bread at the stalls smelled like heaven.'
clues.redirect: No one buys or sells at stalls here. What does the writer want?
clues.why: Crier Pip, crowds and bread at the stalls mean the market.

clues.text: Carry this thank-you to the place it is meant for: 'Hesper, you kept every page of that old map safe and dry. I could not have finished without you.'
clues.redirect: No shelves of old records are kept here. Read the note again.

redirects.object:notice-board: Signs are pinned up on this for passers-by, but nothing is shelved here. Read the note again.

clues.why: Hesper keeps old maps safe and dry in the library.

clues.text: Carry this thank-you to the place it is meant for: 'Mason, your lantern guided me down from the hills in the fog last night.'
clues.redirect: No lantern keeps watch on the hills from here. Which place fits every part of the note?

redirects.landmark:puzzle-tower: This tall place is full of puzzles, not a lookout. Which place fits every part of the note?

clues.why: Mason Gerd's lantern over the hills is at the watchtower.

clues.text: Carry this thank-you to the place it is meant for: 'Ivy, your sage cured my cough. I will sit with you on your sunny bench tomorrow.'
clues.redirect: No herbs grow here. What does the writer want?

redirects.object:beehives: These hives are homes for buzzing workers, not herb beds. What does the writer want?

clues.why: Keeper Ivy's sage and sunny bench are in the garden.

clues.text: Carry this thank-you to the place it is meant for: 'My flock was parched, and that long wooden basin at the south edge saved them.'
clues.redirect: This is not where the animals stop for a slurp. Read the note again.

redirects.landmark:well: Old Bram fills pails for people here, not for animals. Read the note again.

clues.why: A long wooden basin for a parched flock, at the south edge, is the water trough.
